problem: Prior semantic mapping either segments each egocentric frame and projects the labels, or projects pixels and then segments a single top-down image. Segment-then-project (semantic SLAM and similar) causes 'label splatter' from egocentric errors at depth boundaries. Project-then-segment throws away high-resolution egocentric detail, so small objects are missed. Spatial-memory navigation agents never evaluate the semantic quality of their maps, and 3D volumetric feature memories cannot scale to building-size scenes.
motivation: Agents that get a tour of a new space (robots, egocentric assistants) need reusable, metric 'what is where' representations for later tasks such as ObjectNav and question answering. The authors observe that neither projecting labels nor projecting pixels works well: the first gives high precision but low recall with boundary noise, the second gives coarse maps. Projecting learned features into a 2D allocentric memory keeps the egocentric detail while letting an allocentric decoder clean up projection noise.
key_idea: Encode egocentric RGB-D frames with a CNN, project the per-pixel features through known pinhole geometry into a 2 cm-resolution top-down memory, update each cell with a spatially shared GRU, and decode top-down semantic labels allocentrically ('encode pixels, project features, decode labels').
insight: Where the projection happens in the pipeline matters most. Projecting intermediate features lets a learned allocentric decoder smooth 'feature splatter' while keeping high-resolution egocentric cues, which is why SMNet mainly gains recall (47.49 vs 40.53 mRecall over Segment→Project) at similar precision. The appendix ablation (Tab. 'different egocentric features') supports this: 256-channel memory with last-layer decoder features gives mIoU 36.49, versus 34.63 for scores, 34.38 for softmax, 34.12 for one-hot labels and 29.03 for low-res 15×20 encoder features. Even one-hot labels passed through the learned GRU+decoder beat the heuristic-tuned Segment→Project (32.49–32.76). For ObjectNav, the ablations show free-space estimation, not semantics, is the main bottleneck. On 771 episodes, GT semantics plus GT free space gives SR 0.6913; predicted semantics with GT free space gives 0.4306; GT semantics with predicted free space gives 0.2153.
method: Egocentric encoder: RedNet (RGB-D indoor segmentation network, SUN-RGBD-pretrained, fine-tuned on MP3D). Last-layer decoder features (240×320×64) are bilinearly upsampled to the 480×640 depth resolution, giving a 64-d feature per pixel.

Egocentric-to-allocentric projector: inverse pinhole projection with the depth, known intrinsics K and pose [R|t] gives world xyz. An orthographic projection P_v then maps xyz to memory cell (u,v). When several points fall in one cell, the highest one is kept (the tallest object is what is visible from above); points more than 50 cm above the camera are discarded to drop ceilings.

Spatial memory: a U×V×256 tensor, one cell per 2 cm×2 cm of floor. Each observed cell is updated independently with a single-layer GRU whose weights are shared across cells, M_uv^(t)=GRU(F_uv^(t), M_uv^(t-1)). This is deliberately not a ConvGRU, so new observations only change local regions.

Map decoder: 5 conv layers with BatchNorm and ReLU at the same resolution as the memory (no up- or down-sampling). It outputs top-down segmentation over 12 common MP3D categories plus void, labelling each cell with the tallest object.

Training: end-to-end cross-entropy with modal supervision (only cells inside the projected viewing frustum). Trained on 20-step segments sampled from human-recorded tours (50 per floor, 3050 train samples), SGD lr 1e-4, batch 8 on 8 Titan XPs, 2-3 days. At test time the map is built from the full ~2500-step tour.

Downstream reuse: (a) ObjectNav with pre-exploration, running open-loop A* (Euclidean heuristic, 0.25 m / 30° neighbours) on a free-space map thresholded from a height map, combined with the predicted semantic goal map; (b) counting QA through a decoder on 5 m×5 m memory crops (21-way classification, 0..19 and 20+), applied as a sliding window over the full memory.

numbers_note: The main task is top-down semantic segmentation, not navigation. The benchmarks are the authors' own MP3D floor split and Replica transfer. ObjectNav is a proof-of-concept in a pre-exploration setting and is not comparable to standard (novel-environment) ObjectNav. The Seg→Proj baseline appears as 32.76 mIoU in Table 1 and 32.49 in the appendix heuristic table. The best ablation row (last layer, 256 channels: mIoU 36.49) differs slightly from the main-table SMNet (36.77). Further ObjectNav rows (a 7-environment, 771-episode subset with GT/predicted semantic and free-space maps, and per-house breakdowns) exist but are ablations and are not listed above.
results: On Matterport3D test floors, SMNet reaches mIoU 36.77 / mBF1 37.02. The strongest baseline, Segment→Project with tuned heuristics, gets 32.76 / 33.21; Semantic SLAM (VoxBlox++ with GT pose) 28.11 / 31.05; Project→Segment 19.96 / 17.33. The oracle Seg GT→Proj upper bound is 59.73 / 54.05. In zero-shot transfer to Replica, SMNet has the best mIoU (43.12 vs 40.77) but not the best mBF1 (45.18 vs Semantic SLAM's 46.71). As a pre-exploration ObjectNav proof-of-concept on Habitat Challenge 2020 val, A* on SMNet maps gets SR 9.658% / SPL 5.714%, rising to SR 31.25% with GT free space. Counting QA beats a prior baseline (27.78% vs 20.83% accuracy).
limitations: Mapping is passive: it assumes a given (human-recorded) trajectory and known camera pose, and does not do active exploration or joint mapping-and-navigation.

It produces 2D semantic (not instance) maps over only 12 categories plus void, labelling only the tallest object per cell. Instance counting is therefore poor and 26% of ObjectNav episodes are out of vocabulary.

Downstream tasks are proof-of-concept only: ObjectNav is open-loop A* with pre-exploration and a heuristic height-threshold free-space map, which is the dominant error source. The dataset also excludes multi-level floors that a single plane cannot split.
